extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, playwrights, and theorists of comedy/humour
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical / literary-theory criteria describing how verbal form, situation and character produce comic effects (Bergson's theory of laughter). Useful for critics, writers, and scholars analyzing or producing humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series-of-events laws applied to language
rubrics_metrics.description: The three general propositions that make a series comic — repetition, inversion, or reciprocal interference — apply equally to series of words as to events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sentences or verbal sequences like scenes: repeating, inverting, or causing their meanings to interfere will tend to produce comic effects. Use this as a high-level checklist when looking for verbal humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic transformation of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase becomes comic if, though reversed, it still makes sense; or if it expresses equally well two independent sets of ideas; or if it has been obtained by transposing an idea into some key other than its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three concrete operations on sentences yield comedy: reversal (maintaining sense), double-meaning within one sentence, and transposition into another stylistic 'key'. Examples are shown throughout as tests when crafting verbal jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (verbal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the subject in place of the object and the object in place of the subject (or otherwise reverse components) to obtain a comic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider simple syntactic swaps to refute or lampoon an idea. Example given: Labiche's exchange about a pipe/terrace inversion. Marked as the least interesting but readily applicable device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference (puns and play upon words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets of ideas are bracketed in the same expression so they jostle one another; ranges from the pun (different sentences coinciding in sound) to the true play upon words (one sentence expressing two different ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish puns (homophonic wordplay — two different sentences masquerading as one) from genuine double-meaning in a single sentence (figurative vs literal usage). Note the aesthetic/ethical nuance: play upon words signals a momentary lapse of language's attention, which is precisely why it amuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (verbal) — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is always obtainable by transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately render an idea in an unexpected register/style (solemn → familiar, familiar → solemn, technical jargon for everyday matters, etc.). You need not present the 'natural' expression if the audience can supply it; presenting only the transposed version often suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposing the solemn into the familiar = parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing solemn, classical, or elevated matters in familiar, modern, or trivial terms produces parody; the clash between register and subject creates comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incongruous, down-to-earth imagery or modern analogies applied to lofty topics (example: ‘the sky… like a lobster being boiled’). Parody can also arise when modern/banal idioms are used for antiquated/poetic subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition as degradation (solemn → trivial) and its inverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition from dignified to mean (degradation) is comic, but the inverse (treating mean as dignified) may be equally or more comic; both are forms of transposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ degradation for mockery or satire; use the inverse—treating small/low things with inflated respectability—for mock-heroic and satirical humour. Both rely on the contrast between expected and actual register/value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (physical transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak of small things as though they were large is to exaggerate; prolonged, systematic exaggeration is comic (foundation of mock-heroic and habitual braggadocio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make systematic overstatement of scale or importance to create humour. Beware that momentary exaggeration may not suffice; prolonged or methodical inflation intensifies the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition upwards in moral value (elevated register for disreputable matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing scandalous or low-class behaviour in the language of utmost 'respectability' yields comic effect by revealing a moral organisation of immorality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use highly respectable diction to describe disreputable acts or low occupations (example: Gogol's official saying 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank'). A single well-chosen word can reveal an entire transpositional system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real vs ideal transposition — irony and humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition between what is and what ought to be yields distinct modes: irony and humour. Irony states what ought to be and pretends it is what is; humour describes what is and pretends it is what ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is oratorical and moralistic (emphasised by an uplift toward an ideal); humour is more 'scientific', dwelling on concrete technical detail and the cold-blooded recording of reality. Choose mode by whether you aim to uplift/attack (irony) or to dissect/detail (humour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional/technical jargon for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday ideas into the technical vocabulary of a profession (or business phraseology into social relations) produces comic dissonance and can reveal character faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply specialised registers to trivial social situations (e.g., treating marriage as a business affair) to expose mechanistic character traits. This technique can reach depth when it uncovers a fault in character rather than merely producing surface incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language as expression of character; comic in words follows comic in situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Language attains laughable results because it is modelled on the human mind; the mechanical, stereotyped elements in language mirror the mechanical elements in character and situation, producing comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ready-made, lifeless or stereotyped linguistic habits as markers of comic potential; comic diction often signals an underlying mechanistic character trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy begins with unsociability (lack of adaptability to society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual who automatically goes his own way without troubling to get into touch with fellow-beings is comic; laughter functions as a social corrective (a kind of 'ragging').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who are rigidly self-contained, inattentive to social norms, or who fail to adapt provide targets for laughter. Aim to show the character's detachment from social tuning for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter implies social intent to humiliate/correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Even aesthetic laughter is not entirely disinterested; it contains an unconscious or unavowed intent, of society, to humiliate and thereby correct the unsociable individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and, if desired, exploit the moral/social corrective aspect of laughter—it's often a gentle punishment intended to reintegrate the rigid actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional detachment of audience is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is incompatible with emotion; a scene that arouses sympathy, fear, or pity cannot induce laughter. For a vice or virtue to be ludicrous it must not arouse feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing comic material around potentially serious faults, arrange circumstances so the audience's emotions are not engaged (e.g., isolate the feeling, keep it from spreading to other traits, render it parasitic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of feeling within character (parasitic feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the feeling in the character isolated—endowed with an independent existence—so it does not impregnate the whole soul; this rigidity prevents sympathy and fosters comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict emotions as compartmentalised, manifesting as puppet-like or mechanical gestures rather than integrated motivations. Examples: Harpagon's greed passing by other feelings without affecting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy directs attention to gestures rather than actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy focuses on gestures (attitudes, automatic movements, language that slips out unawares) rather than on deliberate, goal-directed actions; gesture is automatic and fragmentary whereas action is intentional and involves the whole person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage or write so that the audience notices involuntary, isolated behaviors (tics, habitual phrases, mannerisms) instead of purposive conduct. Gestures are 'explosive' and wake the audience out of sympathy, producing laughter. This distinguishes comic from dramatic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / rigidity / absentmindedness as core comic condition
rubrics_metrics.description: What is essentially laughable is what is done automatically—absentmindedness, rigidity, and systematic automatism are primary sources of comedy; the deeper the absentmindedness, the higher the comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft characters with unconscious contradictions (declaring a rule then exemplifying its breach), involuntary habits, or systematic absentmindedness (Don Quixote as archetype). The comic arises where a person is unaware of the aspect of themselves that makes them laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy aims at types / the general; stock character formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every comic character is a type; comedy depicts the ready-made, mechanical element of personality and thus crystallises individuals into categories or stock characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve high-class comedy, abstract individual quirks into general types that others can recognise and fall into. The more a character embodies a reproducible 'type', the more comic they are likely to appear.
